Triggers.value: People who are related to the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
I can't stop bad things from happening to me
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Derek Tran never anticipated that a routine evening walk back from the hospice would become a threshold he could not step across again. It had been a cold November afternoon, the streetlamps just flickering on, when a man stepped out from behind a delivery truck. Derek remembered the sudden collapse of personal space, the man's ragged, heavy exhale pressing against his face, and the sharp, unmistakable scent of damp wool and cheap menthol that clung to the stranger's jacket. The man's fingers were cold as they brushed Derek's wrist, demanding his wallet and watch. Derek had handed them over, his own breathing shallow, watching the man's shoulders tense as he turned and melted into the alley. The encounter lasted less than a minute, but the silence that followed felt heavier than the violence itself. In the weeks that followed, Derek's mind refused to process the night as a linear story. What returned to him were sharp, unblinking still frames: the streetlight catching the stranger's glasses, the exact curve of the man's jaw, the way the wallet slipped from his own fingers. Sometimes, while hanging laundry or waiting for the kettle to boil, a draft would carry the smell of wet wool or menthol from a passing car or a neighbor's window, and Derek would freeze, his pulse spiking as the scent flooded the room. When the images surfaced, a hot, sudden anger would coil in his chest. He would stand perfectly still, his fists tightening at his sides, furious at the violation, furious at the fragility of his own body. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally unprotected, that no amount of caution could stop terrible things from landing on him. When he listened to police scanners or read about neighborhood robberies, he would feel a quiet, settling conviction that he was uniquely exposed, that someone else with better instincts or different habits would have seen the threat coming or avoided that block entirely. What unsettled him most was the persistent, unshakable sense that the night had been a reflection of his own moral standing, as if the event had been drawn to him by some unspoken flaw in his character. He began to move through his environment with a new, careful geometry. Derek avoided the downtown plaza near his clinic, where the press of strangers felt like a physical threat. He found himself stepping aside or altering his route whenever a man matched the attacker's build or wore a heavy wool coat. In a crowded pharmacy, he would stand near the automatic doors, his eyes tracking every entrance, bracing himself whenever someone exhaled too loudly through a stuffy nose. The demands of his work as a hospital chaplain grew heavier. He used to walk freely through oncology wards and pediatricICU corridors, sitting with families in waiting rooms and quiet courtyards. Over months, he began scheduling visits only in private offices or over the phone. When a grieving spouse sat too close during a conversation, breathing deeply through congestion, Derek would abruptly check his watch and cite a facility conflict. The chaplain's office, once a space of open doors, became a perimeter he had to guard. By spring, the accumulated isolation had grown into a quiet exhaustion. He sat at his dining table one evening, staring at the stack of unanswered emails from colleagues who wondered why he had stepped back from the community grief groups. Derek knew he needed to return to his patients, but he also knew he could not keep walking through the world with his nervous system permanently on alert. He made an appointment with a trauma specialist, not because he expected the memories to vanish, but because he was tired of feeling like a stranger in his own life. He hoped someone might help him carry the rage without letting it dictate his days, and perhaps teach him how to walk through a crowded room without waiting for the worst to happen.
